items.title: ‘No bank is too big to fail’: Inside the Deutsche Bank leaks
items.summary: Josy Joseph, the Indian author and journalist who obtained the Inside Deutsche Bank leak with South African investigative journalist Khadija Sharife, says the series shows a bank that made more money serving the corrupt than ordinary customers. In conversation with Nikita Saxena, he explains how whistleblower data reached him through a veteran lawyer, and why he chose to share custody with Sharife rather than run the project himself. The investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany. Rather than publish the stories themselves, Joseph and Sharife passed the data on to newsrooms around the world (51 partners in 45 countries, over 250 journalists involved), especially the Global South. In his view, most global investigations are Western and hierarchical, with stories written mainly for readers in Europe and the US, while many of the victims of financial crime live in Asia, Africa and Latin America. On the findings, he points to Deutsche Bank’s alleged role in moving up to $675 million linked to the Gupta brothers during South Africa’s state capture. A large part, he says, reached Indian companies that later defaulted on bank loans in India. He also cites Malaysia’s 1MDB scandal and money flows in Colombia, and says the bank repeatedly lied to and misled US and EU authorities about the amount of Russian oligarch money it handled. Joseph argues that deferred prosecution agreements should end, that fines should be big enough to remove any incentive to mislead regulators. He talks about why no institution is too big to fail. items.summary: उत्तर प्रदेश और मध्य प्रदेश की सीमा पर फैला सोनभद्र-सिंगरौली देश के सबसे बड़े कोयला खनन और ताप बिजली उत्पादन क्षेत्रों में से एक है. यहां की जमीन से निकलने वाला कोयला देश के लाखों घरों और उद्योगों को रोशन करता है. विशाल कोयला खदानें, थर्मल पावर प्लांट और उनसे जुड़ा औद्योगिक ढांचा इस क्षेत्र को भारत के ऊर्जा मानचित्र पर एक महत्वपूर्ण स्थान देते हैं. लेकिन इस विकास की एक दूसरी तस्वीर भी है, जो अक्सर राष्ट्रीय बहस से गायब रहती है. यहां रहने वाले लोगों के हिस्से में आ रही है प्रदूषित हवा, दूषित पानी और प्रभावित होती जमीन. कोयला खनन और बिजलीघरों से निकलने वाली धूल और उत्सर्जन वायु प्रदूषण को बढ़ाते हैं. वहीं, फ्लाई ऐश के अनुचित निस्तारण और उसके पानी में मिलने से नदियों, जलाशयों और भूजल की गुणवत्ता पर गंभीर सवाल खड़े हुए हैं. कई वैज्ञानिक अध्ययनों ने इस क्षेत्र में फ्लोराइड और आर्सेनिक, मरकरी, लेड जैसे हानिकारक तत्वों की मौजूदगी दर्ज की है. कुछ इलाकों में फ्लोरोसिस की समस्या भी सामने आई है पूरी एक पीढ़ी पंगु हो रही है और कई लोगों की मौत हुई है. प्रदूषण का असर केवल इंसानों तक सीमित नहीं है. स्थानीय लोगों के मुताबिक, फ्लाई ऐश मिले पानी को पीने से मवेशियों की मौत हुई है. खेती और आजीविका पर भी इसका असर पड़ रहा है. दूसरी ओर, स्वास्थ्य सुविधाओं की कमी लोगों की मुश्किलें और बढ़ाती है. जिन बीमारियों की जांच और इलाज के लिए बेहतर चिकित्सा व्यवस्था चाहिए, उसके लिए कई ग्रामीणों को दूर जाना पड़ता है. इस डॉक्यूमेंट्री में हम उन गांवों तक पहुंचे हैं जहां बिजली और खनिज संसाधनों से देश की अर्थव्यवस्था को ताकत मिलती है, लेकिन स्थानीय लोग बुनियादी सुविधाओं और स्वच्छ पर्यावरण के लिए संघर्ष कर रहे हैं. सवाल सिर्फ प्रदूषण का नहीं, बल्कि जवाबदेही का भी है. आखिर देश की ऊर्जा जरूरतों की कीमत इस क्षेत्र के लोग कब तक चुकाते रहेंगे? क्या विकास का लाभ यहां के लोगों तक भी पहुंचेगा, या उनके हिस्से में सिर्फ प्रदूषण, बीमारी और उपेक्षा ही आएगी? राष्ट्रीय गीत जिन जगहों और भूभागों की बात करता है, वे आज कैसे हैं? प्रोजेक्ट वंदे मातरम के जरिए हम इसी सवाल का जवाब तलाश रहे हैं. ऐसी कहानियों के लिए कई हफ्तों तक जमीन पर रहकर रिपोर्टिंग करनी पड़ती है. यह काम विज्ञापनदाताओं या कॉरपोरेट घरानों के नहीं, बल्कि पाठकों के सहयोग से ही संभव होता है.अगर आप चाहते हैं कि हम देश के इन हिस्सों की कहानियां आप तक लाते रहें, तो प्रोजेक्ट वंदे मातरम का हिस्सा बनें या न्यूज़लॉन्ड्री को सब्सक्राइब करें. जब एक्यूआई हजार के पार पहुंचा तो सीपीसीबी के आंकड़े कहां गायब हो गए डॉक्यूमेंट्री: सांसों में सिलिका- हर साल इस बीमारी से हो रही हजारों मजदूरों की मौत ​आर्सेनिक डॉक्यूमेंट्री: बंगाल के विधवा गांव और मानवाधिकार का सवाल डॉक्यूमेंट्री: फूड चेन में आर्सेनिक और बिगड़ता सामाजिक तानाबाना

items.title: Sonbhadra-Singrauli: The land that gives us light, and the people poisoned with its ash
items.summary: Sonbhadra-Singrauli, on the Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border, is one of India’s largest coal mining and thermal power regions. Its mines and power plants supply electricity to homes and industries across the country. While the coal here lights up millions of homes across India, the people living on top of it say they are paying with their health. Residents describe a side of that story that rarely reaches the national debate, from its polluted air to its contaminated water and degraded soil. Dust and emissions from mining and power plants hang over the region, and the improper disposal of fly ash has raised serious concerns about its rivers, reservoirs and groundwater. Scientific studies have documented fluoride, arsenic, mercury and lead in the region, and fluorosis has been reported in several areas. Locals say livestock have died after drinking water contaminated with fly ash, and that farming and livelihoods are suffering. With few healthcare facilities nearby, many villagers have to travel far for treatment. In this documentary, we visit the villages whose electricity and minerals power the country’s economy, where people still struggle for basic amenities and a clean environment. As much about the environment, the question is also about accountability. How long will the people here pay the price for the country’s energy needs? Will the benefits of “development” ever reach them? This report is part of our effort to report on the geography the national song describes, as it exists today. Stories like this need weeks on the ground, and they depend on readers, not advertisers or corporate backing. items.title: Supreme Court orders constitution of panels of lawyers, sign language interpreters to assist disabled advocates
items.summary: The Supreme Court will set up a permanent committee to address issues concerning the rights of disabled persons, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant announced on Wednesday. CJI Kant also directed the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee to constitute panels of young lawyers and sign language interpreters to assist advocates with disabilities during proceedings before the Court. The announcements were made during a meeting between CJI Kant and Heba Hagrass , the United Nations' Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities at the Supreme Court. Lawyers with disabilities and representatives of civil society also attended the meeting. During the interaction, CJI Kant observed that ensuring the rights of disabled persons is a constitutional obligation and that equality is a fundamental principle of the Constitution. He stressed the need to identify gaps in the implementation of laws and government schemes to ensure that persons with disabilities could exercise their rights in practice. Referring to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, CJI Kant acknowledged the steps taken by the government and the judiciary over the past decade. CJI Kant said that courts could step in when administrative delays prevent persons with disabilities from getting benefits under laws and government schemes. They could direct public authorities to perform their duties and monitor whether those directions were followed. He also highlighted the role of public interest litigation in helping persons with disabilities enforce their rights. CJI Kant referred to Article 142 of the Constitution, which empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary to do complete justice in cases before it. He encouraged the UN officials present to share India's experience in protecting disability rights with other countries. Speaking about steps taken within the judiciary, he referred to reservation for disabled persons in judicial services and the relaxation of qualifying marks for eligible candidates with disabilities. He also encouraged courts across the country to share practices that have helped improve accessibility and inclusion. Officials from the UN human rights office and the UN Resident Coordinator's office in India attended the meeting, along with representatives of Saksham Trust, iProbono, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, the Politics and Disability Forum and Mission Accessibility. items.title: Maharashtra court staff temporarily suspend strike after Bombay High Court intervention
items.summary: Employees across all district and magistrate courts in Maharashtra have temporarily suspended their indefinite strike , which commenced on November 17 over demands for a revised pay hike. The decision to halt the statewide agitation came after an online meeting held on Wednesday with an administrative committee of Bombay High Court judges. A joint communication announcing halt on strike was issued by the Maharashtra State Court Employees Sanghatana (Class-C), the Maharashtra State Judicial Stenographers Association, the State Judicial Bailiffs Employees Sanghantana, and the Class-D Employees Sanghatana on Wednesday. According to the official communication addressed to the Registrar General of the Bombay High Court, the virtual meeting took place in the afternoon today. In Mumbai, the meeting was attended by administrative judges, Justices AS Gadkari , GS Kulkarni , BP Colabawalla and Suman Shyam led by the Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi . A communication from the High Court clarified that the senior-most judges of the benches at Nagpur, Aurangabad and the circuit bench at Kolhapur also participated in the deliberations. The office-bearers stated that they are putting the strike on hold to honor the direct request and assurances made by the judges and to ensure uninterrupted administration of justice across the State's judicial system. The associations said that the final resolution of the dispute now hinges on upcoming talks with the State government. The employee associations have been assured an official meeting with the Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on November 26. Despite this temporary reprieve, the associations made it clear that the strike has not been permanently called off. They have warned that if a satisfactory resolution is not achieved or a concrete Government Resolution (GR) regarding their long-pending demands is not issued by November 26, they reserve the right to resume the agitation. Nearly 34,000 Maharashtra subordinate court staff began an indefinite strike on November 17, disrupting judicial work. Protesting staffers staged demonstrations outside several civil and sessions courts outside court complexes as the agitation got underway. The employees are protesting the State government's ongoing failure to implement a proposed wage increment based firmly on the principle of "equal pay for equal work".

items.title: Take the writ to the district court: An alternative to regional Supreme Court benches
items.summary: On November 4, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay wrote to the Prime Minister seeking a Supreme Court Bench in Chennai, because access under Article 32 has become practically difficult for those far from Delhi. Six days later, Union Minister of State for Law and Justice Arjun Ram Meghwal said that evening courts, sitting beyond regular hours, would be piloted in Delhi, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh. A provision of the Constitution joins them and Parliament has left it unused for 76 years. The central question is whether the Chief Minister's objective can be met without the consent of the Supreme Court. The demand for a Bench is well supported, with the Law Commission's 95th, 125th and 229th Reports and the Parliamentary Standing Committee's 2nd, 6th, 15th, 20th and 133rd Reports among those favouring regional benches. Its difficulty is constitutional. Under Article 130, the Chief Justice of India appoints other places of sitting with the approval of the President. The Full Court rejected the proposal in August 2007 and reiterated its position in February 2010. A 2016 reference to a Constitution Bench is still pending. The Prime Minister cannot grant what the letter seeks. Article 32(3) offers a route that does not depend on that consent. Structurally, it has three components. First, parliament may by law empower “any other court” to exercise the Supreme Court's powers under clause (2), which are the powers to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights. Second, the court acts only “within the local limits of its jurisdiction”. Third, the powers may be conferred in part, since the words are “all or any”. Article 35 reserves such a law to Parliament. The jurisdiction would, therefore, concern Part III, chiefly Article 21. It would not replicate the wider jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226. Parliament has made no such law. The history is instructive. In the Constituent Assembly on December 9, 1948 , Naziruddin Ahmad asked why a poor litigant should be driven to the Supreme Court. Dr BR Ambedkar replied, “See sub-clause (3).” Rohini Kumar Chaudhuri welcomed the clause for distant places such as Assam and Coorg, while urging that it be used sparingly. Makhan Singh (1964) holds that clause (3) merely confers the Court's powers under clause (2); the guarantee in clause (1) cannot be claimed in respect of other courts. items.title: Foreigners accused of visa overstay can't be kept in detention centres after getting bail: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has ruled that foreign nationals accused of overstaying their visas cannot be directed to remain in detention centres as a condition for being granted bail. A Bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj said that imposing such a condition would defeat the very purpose of granting bail. It added that foreign nationals accused of violating immigration laws are entitled to be considered for bail in the same manner as other criminal accused. “A direction imposing a condition wherein the foreign national is restricted to a detention centre would frustrate the very order of bail and hence, cannot be imposed. Such a power can be exercised by the Central Government by an order under Section 3(2)(g) of the 1946 Act [Foreigners Act], or under Paragraph 8 of the Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025,” the Court said. However, it clarified that granting bail does not legalise a foreign national's continued stay in India or operate as a substitute for a valid visa. Justice Navin Chawla and Arun Bhardwaj of Delhi High Court The High Court made the observations in a criminal reference arising from a bail application filed by a Nigerian national accused of overstaying his tourist visa. He had entered India in 2016 on a three-month visa but continued to reside in the country after its expiry. The reference was made by a Saket court magistrate, who sought clarity on whether granting unconditional bail to such foreign nationals would effectively allow them to stay in India without valid visas and whether they could be kept in detention centres during trial. After considering the case, the High Court ruled that granting bail to a foreign national accused under Section 14 or 14A of the Foreigners Act, 1946 (or the corresponding Section 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025) does not legalise their continued stay in India or operate as a substitute for a valid visa. The trial court had also asked the High Court to answer whether cases involving foreigners charged with overstaying their visas be treated differently from other criminal cases. The Bench said no, adding that persons accused of such an offence must be treated like other criminal accused while considering their bail applications. Advocate Harsh Prabhakar acted as amicus curiae in the matter. He was assisted by advocates Pallavi Garg, Yash Kotak, Dhruv Chaudhry, Shubham Sourav and Vijit Singh. items.title: Come to Delhi from Singapore only after AQI improves: Supreme Court's candid advice for litigant

A Bench of Justices Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan advised a father not to bring his Singapore-based son to the national capital until pollution levels improve. The Court was hearing a contempt of court petition arising out of a long-running matrimonial and custody battle, in which the Delhi-based father had alleged that his estranged wife took their children to Singapore in violation of his court-ordered visitation rights. Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice KV Viswanathan During the hearing, the Bench interacted directly with the estranged couple and their young son - who joined from Singapore - in an effort to rebuild ties between the father and his children. After asking the boy about his elder sister, who is currently in London, Justice Pardiwala playfully noted that she must find time to speak with her brother and told him to convey that "the judges were complaining." The Bench then nudged the father, who lives in Delhi, to travel to Singapore occasionally to visit his son and invite his daughter over for a week to spend time together. When the father welcomed the suggestion and added that it would also be lovely if his son could visit him in Delhi during his school vacations, Justice Pardiwala stepped in with a smile. items.title: Dispute over posthumous release of Siddhu Moose Wala's Phantom Ferrari song: Delhi HC refers case to mediation
items.summary: A dispute over whether music label Saga Music holds the rights to release the video of the "Phantom Ferrari" song sung by late singer Siddhu Moose Wala posthumously has been referred to mediation by the Delhi High Court. Siddhu Moose Wala’s parents have opposed the song's release, arguing that their permission has not been taken for releasing the song. On the other hand, Saga Music has asserted that the song's copyright was assigned to it by Moose Wala before his demise. Justice Manoj Jain today urged the parties to try and settle the dispute amicable manner. "Your son enjoys popularity sitting in heaven… It is better advised for both parties to find an amicable solution," the judge said, addressing the parents' counsel. The counsel said that he had no objection if the matter is referred to mediation. He also assured the Court that the parents will not issue any further statements to aggravate the dispute for the timebeing. "The counsel for the defendants assures that till the next date of hearing, defendant No 2 and 3 (Moose Wala's parents) shall not isssue any further statement aggravating or precipitating the issue in any manner whatsoever. Further, no further precipitative steps shall be taken with respect to the song in question," the Court's order stated. With the consent of the parties, the Court proceeded to refer the dispute to mediation. The mediation process has been scheduled to begin on November 23. The Court will hear the matter next on December 3. Justice Manoj Jain Saga Music has filed a suit in the matter, maintaining that a copyright assignment agreement was executed with Moose Wala in 2020, whereby his rights in the song 'Phantom Ferrari' were transferred to the music label. Saga Music uploaded a teaser on YouTube announcing that the full track would be released on November 13, 2026. items.title: TVK under fire after cadres open Theni dam outlet without govt order, share videos
items.summary: The ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) is facing criticism after some of its functionaries allegedly opened a water outlet connected to the Sothuparai dam in Theni district without the knowledge or permission of government officials and shared videos of the incident on social media. The incident took place on Tuesday, November 17, near Periyakulam, where the functionaries, led by TVK's Theni North-East district joint secretary Sheikh Ali, opened a water outlet in an irrigation channel, claiming that they had acted on the instructions of Periyakulam MLA Sabari Aingaran to benefit around 1,000 acres of farmland. Water Resources Department (WRD) officials told The Hindu that the functionaries had not opened the main shutters of the Sothuparai dam. Instead, they opened a water outlet in the New Canal located around 1.5 km downstream of the dam to divert excess water overflowing from the reservoir. It has to be noted that the irrigation structure was under the direct control of the WRD and that no outsider could operate it without permission. The incident came to light after the videos circulated on social media, prompting Theni Collector V Sivakrishnamurthy to direct department officials to file a police complaint. Following the Collector's instructions, the Assistant Engineer of the Water Resources Department, Manoj, lodged a complaint at the Thenkarai police station seeking action against those who opened the water outlet without permission. Sothuparai dam, built across the Varagha River in Periyakulam taluk, has a full storage capacity of around 126.28 feet. It is an important drinking water source for nearly two lakh people in Periyakulam and surrounding areas, and also provides irrigation to around 2,856 acres of farmland in the region, including areas in Kailasapatti, Lakshmipuram, Vadugapatti, Melmangalam and Jayamangalam. Water is usually released from the dam for irrigation around November following a government order, in the presence of elected representatives, the district Collector and Water Resources Department officials. However, no such government order had been issued this year. According to officials, excess water had been flowing out of the dam since October 23. However, it could not be diverted through the new irrigation channel earlier because the channel was overgrown with plants and bushes and the clearing work was completed only recently. items.title: Opinion: A fair umpire cannot fix India's tilted electoral playing field
items.summary: The country is arguing about its umpire. As this is written, the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is facing petitions in the Supreme Court and demands for his resignation. Fair umpiring matters, and it must be secured. But even a perfect umpire cannot fix the rules of the game. On a tilted pitch, the most honest umpire in the world will only preside fairly over an unfair match. I belong to the generation that let the pitch tilt. We complained at dinner tables and voted for the same symbols. The people we elected grew richer, their criminal cases grew heavier, and we learned to call it normal. The young have stopped calling it normal. When some of them were dismissed as cockroaches, they turned the insult into a movement that reached millions within days, on almost no money. I am proud of them. Only the young, it seems, still have the courage and the energy to ask uncomfortable questions of those in power. So I have written down the questions I believe go to the root, as a letter I hope they will make their own: to their elders, to those in power, and to our courts. The questions are theirs to ask. The answers belong to all of us. Here’s the letter: QUESTIONING OUR ELECTIONS FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES 1. Increasing criminality in electoral politics Why do so many of our elected representatives face serious criminal charges? These are not minor cases. The Association for Democratic Reforms counts a case as serious if the offence carries a maximum sentence of five years or more, is non-bailable, or involves charges such as murder, kidnapping, crimes against women, or corruption. In 2024, 31% of elected MPs, nearly one in three, declared serious criminal cases against themselves, up from 14% in 2009. Why is this number rising? If an election is meant to choose the best among us, its filtering function clearly seems a bit broken. Why is it failing to reduce the number of candidates with serious criminal cases? Only when the legal system convicts an elected representative does the system take the face-saving step of removing them. items.title: Waste picker in Bengaluru set ablaze after being tied up, in critical condition
items.summary: A 45-year-old waste picker is in critical condition after unidentified persons allegedly tied him up, poured petrol on him, and set him ablaze on a road in Veerabhadranagar, south Bengaluru, in the early hours of Wednesday, November 18. The victim, identified as Mohammed alias Syed H, was found by area residents around 6 am, with severe burn injuries. They alerted the police through the emergency helpline 112. A Hoysala patrol team reached the spot and arranged for an ambulance to shift him to Victoria Hospital, where he is undergoing treatment. According to the police, Mohammed has suffered 60-70% burns. His hands and legs were allegedly tied with ropes before he was set on fire. Mohammed collects scrap for a living and has no permanent shelter, mobile phone, or identity documents. He reportedly sleeps on the roadside and had been staying in the Padarayanapura area for several years. Girinagar police visited the spot and are investigating the incident. A case is being registered, the police said.

items.title: Manaveeyam Veedhi: Why artists in Kerala are fighting with a BJP Mayor for this street
items.summary: A lane in Thiruvananthapuram that has been a cultural corridor for 25 years, fondly called Manaveeyam Veedhi (Street of Humanity), is tangled up in a controversy over the city Corporation’s incursions. In the span of a month, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation, ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), filed a case against organisers of a protest gathering and denied permission for another musical performance. The protest, held in October, in which actor and activist Prakash Raj participated, demanded the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, echoing the youth movement in Delhi. Voices were being raised across the country against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls conducted by the Election Commission, that excluded crores of valid voters. In Thiruvananthapuram, nine organisers of the protest, called Collective for Democracy, were charged for holding the gathering without prior permission. BJP leader and Mayor VV Rajesh reportedly said that the action was only procedural and not politically motivated. But that is not true, and the criteria for granting permissions is evidently political, according to KG Suraj, convenor of the Manaveeyam Samskarika Koottayma. “The Corporation is imposing a mandate that you need its permission to conduct events on that street. But the way permissions are granted, it is clearly political. While they got the organisers of the anti-SIR protest booked, they had allowed another event which was in support of the SIR. This was a ‘padayathra’ organised by the BJP, in which the stage was actually jutting out on the road, instead of the wide footpath where it is usually placed,” says Suraj. Hardly a month after the anti-SIR protest organisers were booked, the Corporation denied permission to another event in connection with the silver jubilee celebrations of Manaveeyam Veedhi.
